issues.legal_issue: A secured creditor’s application for magistrate assistance to take possession of secured assets is an enforcement measure reviewable by the Debts Recovery Tribunal.
material_facts: A bank sought possession of mortgaged properties through an application to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate under the statutory possession-assistance procedure.
The Magistrate allowed the application, and an officer acting under the Magistrate’s order notified the borrowers to hand over possession.
The borrowers challenged the possession action.
issues.conclusion: An action under Section 14 occurs after the stage contemplated by Section 13(4) and falls within the scope of an application to the Debts Recovery Tribunal under Section 17.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 13(4), 14 and 17 of the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002, permit a secured creditor to use the magistrate’s assistance to enforce its possession rights, and allow an aggrieved person to challenge measures taken under Section 13(4) before the Debts Recovery Tribunal. The Court applied Authorised Officer, Indian Overseas Bank v. Ashok Saw Mill, which held that the Tribunal may review post-Section 13(4) actions and grant appropriate relief, including restoration of possession; it also referred to United Bank of India v. Satyawati Tondon.

predicates.secured_asset_enforcement_proceeding: A secured creditor is pursuing enforcement of its security interest against secured assets.
predicates.creditor_sought_magistrate_assistance_fo: The secured creditor asked a magistrate to assist in taking possession of secured assets.

issues.definition: When enforcement of secured assets involves a creditor seeking magistrate assistance to take possession, the resulting possession action is reviewable by the debt tribunal.

issues.legal_issue: A constitutional writ court may decline to intervene in a challenge to secured-asset enforcement when an effective statutory appeal is available, particularly where the dispute involves contested facts.
material_facts: The borrowers challenged notices and possession-related steps in a writ petition.
The dispute included contested claims about whether a notice had been received and whether the Magistrate’s order had been communicated.
A statutory appeal to the Debts Recovery Tribunal was available, and the borrowers ultimately pursued that remedy.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in declining to exercise its writ jurisdiction because an efficacious statutory remedy was available and the dispute involved questions of fact.
issues.legal_principle: Relief under Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution is ordinarily unavailable where an efficacious alternative remedy exists; the availability of such a remedy and the presence of disputed factual questions are relevant considerations in deciding whether to exercise writ jurisdiction. The Court relied on Sadhana Lodh v. National Insurance Co. Ltd., Surya Dev Rai v. Ram Chander Rai, State Bank of India v. Allied Chemical Laboratories, and City and Industrial Development Corporation v. Dosu Aardeshir Bhiwandiwala.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A person asks a constitutional writ court to set aside or restrain an enforcement action.
predicates.effective_statutory_appeal_available: The person has an effective statutory appeal available to challenge the action.
predicates.material_factual_disputes_present: The challenge turns in part on contested factual matters.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ challenge concerns contested facts and an effective statutory appeal is available, the writ court may decline intervention.
